text:
Development-process differences by approach

Scope: Because the platform is unidentified, this comparison is platform-neutral.

Approach | How development changes | Primary validation
Modularization | Teams first define domain boundaries, ownership, interfaces, and shared libraries. Modules can then be designed, implemented, and released independently. | Unit tests, contract tests, dependency checks, and cross-module integration tests.
System integrations | Developers map source and destination formats, build adapters or connectors, and explicitly handle transformation, latency, retries, and external-system limitations. | Sandbox tests, integration tests, malformed-message tests, and external-system failure simulations.
API gateway | Teams design API contracts and lifecycle rules before implementation, then configure routing, authentication, throttling, validation, and versioning separately from business logic. | Contract, authorization, rate-limit, compatibility, and performance tests.
Databases | Development includes data modeling, ownership rules, migration scripts, transaction boundaries, and strategies for replication, backup, and retention. | Migration, integrity, concurrency, rollback, recovery, and performance tests.
Security | Threat modeling and control definition begin during design rather than after coding. Identity, permissions, secrets, encryption, and auditability become acceptance criteria for every feature. | Security scanning, access-control tests, penetration tests, dependency checks, and audit verification.
Business workflows | Teams model states, transitions, approvals, timers, retries, and compensating actions before implementing individual tasks. Business rules are separated from orchestration where practical. | End-to-end path, timeout, retry, duplicate-event, exception, and compensation tests.
Observability | Developers add structured logs, metrics, traces, correlation identifiers, dashboards, and alert conditions as part of each feature rather than as later operational work. | Telemetry completeness, trace propagation, dashboard, and alert tests.
Delivery automation | Build, test, configuration, infrastructure, deployment, promotion, and rollback steps are encoded in version-controlled pipelines. Changes must pass automated quality gates. | Pipeline, environment-parity, deployment, smoke, rollback, and infrastructure-policy tests.
Resilience | Failure behavior is designed explicitly through asynchronous processing, idempotency, retries, circuit breakers, caching, scaling, and recovery objectives. | Load, failover, chaos, duplicate-request, degraded-dependency, and disaster-recovery tests.
Governance | Teams use approved templates, standards, catalogs, dependency records, compliance controls, and named lifecycle owners. Reviews and evidence collection become part of normal delivery. | Architecture checks, policy-as-code, ownership verification, dependency audits, and compliance evidence reviews.

issues: The historical claim lacks a valid prior user citation: The previously provided answer covered modularization, integrations, API gateways, databases, security, workflows, observability, delivery automation, resilience, and governance.

limitations: Exact workflows and tooling depend on the platform, architecture, team structure, scale, and compliance requirements.
